assumptions: Each project is a binary decision: either selected once or not selected.
Project cost, labor, and value are additive across selected projects.
The objective is to maximize total value subject to budget and labor limits.
An empty selection is allowed because no rule forbids selecting zero projects.

baseline.description: Simple manual baseline: choose the single project with the highest standalone value.
evidence: Among single-project choices, A has the largest value (11) while remaining feasible with cost 6 and labor 4.
This baseline is feasible but inferior to the enumerated optimum AB with value 19.

candidate_models: Exact exhaustive enumeration over all binary project subsets.
claims: Verified: the optimization problem can be modeled with four binary decision variables and two linear resource constraints.
Verified: exhaustive enumeration over all 16 subsets yields AB as the best feasible selection with objective value 19.
Verified: the single-project baseline value is 11 from selecting A only.
Verified: some greedy heuristics are suboptimal on this instance, while greedy-by-value happens to match the optimum.
Inference: exhaustive enumeration is the most appropriate model among the tested candidates because the instance is very small and exact search is cheap.
code_artifacts: Inline Python enumerator executed from the shell; no repository file was created.
commands_executed: python3 - <<'PY' ... exhaustive subset enumeration over 16 masks ... PY
data_findings: Input parameters read from case/input/problem.json: budget=10, labor_capacity=7.
Projects: A(cost 6, labor 4, value 11), B(4,3,8), C(5,4,10), D(3,2,6).
Units from input: cost=credit, labor=worker-day, value=benefit-point.
Exhaustive enumeration checked all 16 subsets of the 4 projects.
Feasible high-value subsets include AB(value 19), BC(value 18), AD(value 17), CD(value 16), BD(value 14).
The best feasible subset found by enumeration is AB with total cost 10, labor 7, value 19.
experiment_design: Use the local JSON input as the sole data source.
Compute a trivial baseline from standalone project values.
Run exhaustive enumeration to obtain the exact optimum.
Run several simple greedy heuristics as candidate approximate models and compare their outputs to the exact optimum.
falsification_tests: If any omitted feasible subset had value greater than 19, the optimality claim would be false; the full 16-subset listing is intended to rule this out.
If project decisions were not binary or if partial projects were allowed, this formalization would be false.
If the input implied hidden dependencies or mutual exclusions not represented in the JSON, the enumerated optimum could be invalid.

constraints: Binary decision constraint: x_i in {0,1} for each listed project.
notes: This is a 0-1 knapsack-style selection problem with two resource constraints.
Because there are only 4 projects, exhaustive search is tractable and sufficient to identify the optimum exactly.
parameters: For each project i: cost c_i, labor l_i, value v_i from the input table.
units: Objective value is measured in benefit-point.
Budget consumption is measured in credit.
Labor consumption is measured in worker-day.
variables: x_A, x_B, x_C, x_D in {0,1}, where x_i=1 means project i is selected.

reality_constraints: Labor capacity is limited to 7 worker-day.
Only the four listed projects A, B, C, and D are available.
No stochastic effects, dependencies, or partial-project choices are provided in the input.
requirements: Read TASK.json, runtime_metadata.json, ARM_INSTRUCTION.md, case/input/problem.json, and observation.schema.json from the isolated repository.
Work without network, MCP, remotes, parent directories, credentials, or historical material.
Define variables, parameters, objective, constraints, and units for the optimization problem.
Implement and actually run an enumerator.
Compare the enumerator with candidate models and state falsification conditions.
Return exactly one JSON object matching observation.schema.json.
robustness_tests: Compared the exact solution against multiple greedy rules to check whether the optimum was heuristic-dependent.
Observed that some heuristics miss the optimum on this instance (value/cost, value/labor, lowest-cost-first), supporting the need for exact enumeration at this scale.
Observed that greedy-by-value matches the optimum here, but only as an empirical coincidence on this input, not as a proven general rule.
selected_model: Exact exhaustive enumeration over all 2^4 project subsets.
self_reported_limitations: No repository files were added for reusable code; the enumerator was executed inline.
The analysis is limited strictly to the provided local input and does not address larger-instance scalability beyond noting that exhaustive search is tractable for 4 projects.
sources_used: Local shell execution results from inline Python commands run inside the repository.
tests_claimed: Verified that exhaustive enumeration visited all 16 subsets implied by 4 binary decisions.
Verified feasibility checks against both budget and labor constraints.
Verified that the reported optimum AB is feasible and has larger value than every other feasible subset listed by the enumerator.
Verified candidate greedy heuristics against the same input for comparison.
tests_verified: The enumerator output listed all subsets from EMPTY through ABCD, confirming coverage of 16 combinations.
The enumerator reported AB with cost 10 and labor 7 as feasible and value 19 as the maximum among feasible subsets.
Greedy-by-value also returned AB with value 19 on this instance.
Greedy-by-value/cost returned BC with value 18, greedy-by-value/labor returned DA with value 17, and lowest-cost-first returned DB with value 14.
uncertainties: No external solver or third-party validator was used; conclusions rely on the local enumeration run.
Schema conformance was constructed carefully from the provided schema, but no separate JSON-schema validation tool was run.
validation: The exact optimum is supported by explicit enumeration of every possible subset.
Feasibility of AB is validated directly: cost 6+4=10 <= 10 and labor 4+3=7 <= 7.
Optimality of AB is validated because every other feasible subset in the enumerator output has value <= 18.
